history.hypothesis: DirectoryManagerFactory holds the chosen manager class in a static field; the sibling test createDirectoryManagerNoConstructor sets it to TestDirectoryManager (a no-op that never throws IOException), so if it runs before createDirectoryManagerIoException the victim's expected IOException is never raised and the test fails.

diagnosis.root_cause: DirectoryManagerFactory stores the configured DirectoryManager implementation in a static field. The preceding test createDirectoryManagerNoConstructor sets that static field to TestDirectoryManager, which has no (Path, Boolean) constructor. When createDirectoryManagerIoException later runs in the same JVM, reflection attempts to instantiate the stale TestDirectoryManager and throws a RuntimeException/NoSuchMethodException before the code can reach the expected IOException path.

evidence.why: This polluting test mutates the shared static factory class state to TestDirectoryManager, leaving it configured for subsequent tests.
TestDirectoryManager defines only the default no-arg constructor, so it does not have the (java.nio.file.Path, java.lang.Boolean) constructor that DirectoryManagerFactory reflection requires.

This test calls createDirectoryManager with the stale TestDirectoryManager still registered. Reflection on its missing constructor throws RuntimeException, so JUnit reports expected IOException but got RuntimeException.

diagnosis.root_cause: The static counter PrimitiveChars.iterations is never reset at the end of the primitiveChars test, unlike the other tests in this file which do `PrimitiveBooleans.iterations = 0;`. When the same JVM executes the test a second time (runs:2), each JUnitQuickcheck EXHAUSTIVE property execution adds defaultPropertyTrialCount() (100) iterations to the already-nonzero static field, so the second run sees 200 instead of 100.

evidence.why: The assertion at L165 (the failing line in the stack) compares the ever-accumulating static counter to defaultPropertyTrialCount(); since the test never resets PrimitiveChars.iterations, a second in-JVM execution doubles the value to 200.
The static field `iterations` is process-wide mutable state that is incremented on every property trial and never cleared, so repeated executions in the same JVM accumulate (100 -> 200).

Contrast: primitiveBooleans (and primitiveBytes) explicitly reset their static counter to 0 at the end of the test, preventing cross-execution accumulation; primitiveChars omits this reset, which is exactly what causes the non-idempotent 200 result.

The JVM-wide static state makes the test non-idempotent across repeated in-JVM executions.

The test asserts a full serialized JSON string with a fixed key order (op, path, value), but a HashMap can emit path, value, op, causing the assertion to fail nondeterministically depending on JVM hash ordering of the string keys.

evidence.why: The test compares the entire serialized JSON string against a literal with a specific key ordering. The observed failure shows the same values but reordered keys (path,value,op instead of op,path,value), proving the assertion is sensitive to Map iteration/serialization order rather than to the data itself.

evidence.why: The patch command is assembled into a Map (e.g., a HashMap) whose entries are serialized by the JSON serializer in hash-bucket order. diagnosis.root_cause: The test asserts equality against a hard-coded JSON string whose object keys are in a fixed order (op, path, value), but the actual serialized output emits the same keys in a different order (path, value, op). The JSON is produced by reflecting over the patch/command object (or an un-ordered Map), and the field/property enumeration order returned by the JVM reflection API is not guaranteed to be stable across JVM runs, so the serialized key order varies nondeterministically.

evidence.why: The assertion compares the serialized hook against a literal JSON string with a fixed key order. The reproduced failure shows the actual output had the same fields but ordered as path,value,op instead of op,path,value, so the assertion fails purely on key ordering rather than on content.

history.hypothesis: The expected string is built by SDKVersion.getLibraryString(), while the actual string comes from Gson reflecting over CastleSdkRef fields; if either relies on hash-based collection iteration order (e.g. a Map used to assemble the library JSON), the two orderings can differ and the equality assertion fails non-deterministically. Perturbing JDK hash/iteration order with NonDex should expose it.

diagnosis.root_cause: Gson serializes model objects by reflecting over the class's declared fields, and Class.getDeclaredFields() returns fields in an unspecified, JVM-run-dependent order. The test builds the expected JSON string with a fixed field order (active, then library{name,version,platform,platform_version}), but model.getGson().toJson(aContext) emits the fields of CastleContext and CastleSdkRef in whatever reflective order the JVM happens to return for that run, so the serializer output is nondeterministically permuted.

evidence.snippet: Assertions.assertThat(contextJson).isEqualTo("{\"active\":true," + SDKVersion.getLibraryString() +"}");
evidence.why: This is the failing assertion (stack line CastleContextTest.java:29). It compares the Gson-serialized object against a hard-coded field order, so any permutation of field order produced by Gson's reflective serialization causes a ComparisonFailure.

evidence.snippet: CastleContext aContext = new CastleContext(); String contextJson = model.getGson().toJson(aContext); Assertions.assertThat(contextJson).isEqualTo(...);
evidence.why: The actual value comes from model.getGson().toJson(aContext), which serializes CastleContext and its nested CastleSdkRef library object using Class.getDeclaredFields(). Field order from reflection is not specified by the JVM, explaining the observed per-run permutations of active/library and of the library sub-fields (name, version, platform, platform_version).

evidence.snippet: returns a literal library JSON fragment with fixed order name, version, platform, platform_version
evidence.why: The expected string assumes a fixed key order (name,version,platform,platform_version), while the observed failures show this exact set of keys reordered (e.g. platform_version,platform,version,name), confirming the mismatch is purely ordering of the reflected fields, not values.

history.hypothesis: The test builds JSON where array/map element ordering depends on HashMap/HashSet iteration order, so a hash-seed perturbation (NonDex) will change the serialized output and make the string comparison assertion fail again, revealing the order-dependence.

diagnosis.root_cause: The test asserts exact string equality on a JSON document whose inner patch-operations object is serialized from a HashMap (or other unordered Map) rather than an ordered structure. Iteration order of the operation's keys (op, path, value) is derived from the key hash codes, so the serialized key order is nondeterministic across JVM/round executions and does not match the hard-coded expected string.

evidence.snippet:
def json = JsonOutput.toJson(hooks)
assertThat(json, is("{\"commands\":[{\"type\":\"com.okta.assertion.patch\",\"value\":[{\"op\":\"replace\",\"path\":\"/claims/array/attributeValues/1/value\",\"value\":\"replacementValue\"}]}]}"))
evidence.why: The test compares the full JSON string, including the order of keys inside the patch-operation object, to a hard-coded literal. Because the assertion depends on key ordering it fails whenever the serializer emits the keys in a different order (observed: path,value,op vs op,path,value).

The operation is emitted as a HashMap, whose iteration order is determined by key hash codes and is not insertion-ordered. This is the concrete source of the nondeterministic key ordering that the test's exact-string assertion trips over.

history.hypothesis: The recursive ToStringStyle keeps per-thread/static visited-object state keyed by identity hash, so hash-order perturbations can alter the rendered char-array output; NonDex's nondeterminism injection should expose this.

diagnosis.root_cause: MultilineRecursiveToStringStyle builds the output by reflecting over the fields of WithArrays and emitting them in the order returned by the reflection API, which is unspecified (JVM/HashMap-free but implementation-dependent and subject to variation). The test hard-codes the expected field order (boolArray, charArray, intArray, doubleArray, longArray, stringArray), so whenever reflection yields a different ordering the assertion fails, even though the object state is identical.

evidence.snippet: final String exp = getClassPrefix(wa) + "[" + BR + "  boolArray=<null>," + BR + "  charArray={" ... + "  stringArray=<null>" + BR + "]"; assertEquals(exp, toString(wa));
evidence.why: The expected string fixes the field order, while the actual output in the failure (stringArray first, or longArray first, etc.) shows a different order each run, so the assertion fails nondeterministically.

evidence.snippet: assertEquals(exp, toString(wa));
evidence.why: Stack trace points exactly here; the mismatch is purely ordering of the reflected fields, not values, confirming reflection order dependence.

evidence.snippet: final Field[] fields = getFields(); ... for (final Field field : fields) { ... appendFields ... }
evidence.why: Field iteration uses getDeclaredFields() whose order is not guaranteed to match declaration order across JVMs/runs, producing the varying order observed in the actual output.

history.hypothesis: This serialization test compares a JSON string produced by serializing BillDeskOnlineDetails (likely via Gson/Jackson over fields backed by a HashMap), so iteration order of hash-based collections can vary between JVM runs and produce a mismatching string; NonDex will perturb JDK hash ordering and expose this nondeterminism.

diagnosis.root_cause: The reproduced failure is not from the serialization test itself but from com.adyen.util.CertificateUtilTest#testLoadKeyStore, which throws FileNotFoundException because the shared classpath resource target/test-classes/testStore.keystore is no longer present at the time it runs. Since Maven copies this resource once into target/test-classes before the suite starts, its disappearance can only be caused by a previously executed test in the same JVM mutating/deleting that shared file, so any later test execution in the same JVM observes a mutated environment and fails.

evidence.snippet: certificateUtil.loadKeyStore(...) // testLoadKeyStore
evidence.why: This test reads the shared resource testStore.keystore from the classpath; when a prior test has deleted/mutated it, the read fails with FileNotFoundException.

evidence.snippet: throw new FileNotFoundException("Keystore file not found at path " + path)
evidence.why: CertificateUtil.loadKeyStore assumes the keystore file exists at the given path; it does not recreate or restore the resource, so the missing file surfaces as the observed failure.

evidence.snippet: public class CheckoutTest extends BaseTest { ... TestBillDeskOnlineDetailsSerialization ... }
evidence.why: CheckoutTest runs in the same JVM/suite as CertificateUtilTest and its serialization helpers touch shared, mutable static state and files; ordering of these tests within the JVM therefore dictates whether the shared keystore resource is still intact, making the outcome non-idempotent across repeated executions.

history.hypothesis: Both a fresh isolated rerun (T1) and an order-perturbed run (T5) fail identically on the WithArrays field rendering, so the flakiness is intrinsic nondeterminism in how ReflectionToStringBuilder/MultilineRecursiveToStringStyle enumerates the declared fields of WithArrays (hash/iteration-order sensitive rather than test-order or timing sensitive); NonDex perturbation of JDK hash order should expose a reordered or scrambled field listing that reproduces the mismatch.

diagnosis.root_cause: The assertion hard-codes the field order of WithArrays (boolArray, charArray, intArray, doubleArray, longArray, stringArray), but the actual text is generated via reflection (ReflectionToStringBuilder -> Class.getDeclaredFields), whose returned order is not specified by the JVM and can vary between runs/JIT states. The failure messages show the same fields and values merely permuted (e.g. intArray first, or boolArray/stringArray/doubleArray reordered), so the test depends on nondeterministic reflection ordering rather than on any real behavioral bug.

evidence.snippet: public void boolArray() { final WithArrays wa = new WithArrays(); wa.boolArray = new boolean[] { true, false, true }; final String exp = getClassPrefix(wa) + "[" + BR + "  boolArray={" ... "  charArray=<null>," + BR + "  intArray=<null>," ... assertEquals(exp, toString(wa)); }
evidence.why: The expected string fixes the field order boolArray,charArray,intArray,doubleArray,longArray,stringArray, but the produced string is compared verbatim; any different reflection order fails the assertion even though values are identical.

evidence.snippet: assertEquals(exp, toString(wa));
evidence.why: This is the exact line reported in the reproduced failure stack; the diff is only in the ordering of the six reflected fields (e.g. 'intArray=<null>, boolArray={...}, charArray=<null>, stringArray=<null>, doubleArray=<null>, longArray=<null>'), proving order-dependence on reflection.

evidence.snippet: private String getClassPrefix(final Object object) { return object.getClass().getName() + "@" + Integer.toHexString(System.identityHashCode(object)); } ... public String toString() { return ReflectionToStringBuilder.toString(this, ...); }
evidence.why: toString() delegates to reflection-based field enumeration; Class.getDeclaredFields() order is unspecified, so the emitted field order (and thus the compared string) is implementation dependent and can change across runs.

history.hypothesis: The serialization test compares an exact JSON string against the model's serialized output, and the field ordering produced by the Gson/Jackson serializer depends on non-deterministic JDK hash/reflection ordering, so perturbing hash ordering should make the output mismatch the expected literal.

diagnosis.root_cause: The failing tests serialize a request object to JSON and compare the resulting string byte-for-byte against a hard-coded expected JSON whose field order is fixed (amount first). The actual serialized output places the fields in a different order (merchantAccount/applicationInfo/returnUrl before amount, etc.), meaning the backing data structure used during serialization has a nondeterministic iteration order (a plain HashMap / unordered Map rather than an insertion-ordered Map). Because hash-based iteration order varies across JVM runs (and across rounds), the JSON key order flips and the equality assertion on the full string fails intermittently, independent of any other test.

evidence.snippet: assertEquals(expectedJson, gson.toJson(paymentRequest));
evidence.why: Stack trace points to CheckoutTest.java:926 as the failing assertEquals; the ComparisonFailure shows the same key/value pairs but in a different order, i.e. a full-string comparison that is sensitive to serialization field order.

evidence.snippet: expected:<{"amount":{...},"merchantAccount":"TestMerchant",...}> but was:<{"merchantAccount":"TestMerchant",..."amount":{"value":1000,"currency":"GBP"}...}>
evidence.why: The observed diff is purely a reordering of identical keys (amount, merchantAccount, paymentMethod, reference, returnUrl, applicationInfo), which is the signature of HashMap/hash-order-dependent serialization rather than a value change or missing/extra field.

history.hypothesis: The test inspects the result of an aborted write intent through a read path whose outcome depends on JDK-level nondeterminism (hash/iteration order or timestamp ordering inside the storage), so perturbing JDK nondeterminism with a fixed random seed will surface the failing interleaving.

diagnosis.root_cause: The failure never occurs in the test body; it happens during JUnit parameter resolution of setUp (@InjectConfiguration TablesConfiguration arg2), where the Ignite ConfigurationExtension builds/mock-serializes the configuration tree and hits an AssertionError on org.apache.ignite.internal.schema.configuration.index.TableIndexConfigurationSchema. This only surfaces under the T12 multi-round strategy (same JVM, 30 rounds) because the ConfigurationExtension/schema-registry state is mutated on the first resolution and is not reset, so every subsequent execution in the same JVM fails at setUp before the test even runs.

evidence.why: The reproduced stack trace is a ParameterResolutionException for TablesConfiguration arg2 raised inside setUp, so the failure is entirely in ConfigurationExtension's @InjectConfiguration resolution, not in the partition-storage logic; the schema name in the AssertionError (TableIndexConfigurationSchema) belongs to the TablesConfiguration schema, confirming the mock-tree resolution path.

diagnosis.root_cause: The toString output is produced by ReflectionToStringBuilder, which iterates the reflected java.lang.reflect.Field objects of WithArrays. The Field instances are gathered into a hash-based collection (identity-hash-backed), so their iteration order depends on Object.identityHashCode and therefore varies from JVM run to JVM run. The assertion compares an exact multiline string built by the test in declaration order (boolArray, charArray, intArray, doubleArray, longArray, stringArray) against the reflection-produced order, which is shuffled nondeterministically.

selector.requeue();

evidence.why: This is the exact assertion reported at TestLeaderSelectorCluster.java:181; it is a bounded timing wait for the semaphore released by takeLeadership, and it fails when leadership is not re-acquired within the deadline.

Shows the semaphore is only released from inside takeLeadership (which itself already uses timing.multiple(4)), so any delay in the session-LOST/leadership cycle directly lengthens the time before the line-181 assertion can succeed.

diagnosis.root_cause: The test asserts that exactly 20 snapshot-install notifications are observed by the leader/follower, but the snapshot-install and notification-delivery paths run asynchronously in separate gRPC/thread pools. Under load (parallel class execution with 4 threads), the final notification for one of the install attempts races with the assertion: the snapshot has been installed but the corresponding notification has not yet been delivered/counted when assertEquals runs, yielding 19 instead of 20.

evidence.snippet: runWithNewCluster(NUM_SERVERS, this::runTest, ...);
evidence.why: The test spins up a MiniRaftCluster and drives repeated snapshot installs; the entry point that sets up the async install/notification machinery.

evidence.snippet: assertEquals(expectedNotificationCount, notificationCount.get());
evidence.why: The assertion on the count that failed with expected:<20> but was:<19>; it reads the counter before the last asynchronous snapshot-install notification has been observed, so a load-induced delay drops one count.

evidence.snippet: public class TestInstallSnapshotNotificationWithGrpc extends InstallSnapshotNotificationTests<MiniRaftClusterWithGrpc> implements MiniRaftClusterWithGrpc.FactoryGet {}
evidence.why: The gRPC transport delivers install-snapshot notifications on separate threads, so the leader-side counter can lag behind the follower-side install completion — the nondeterministic timing window.

diagnosis.root_cause: The three MyCoordActionInputCheckXCommand instances all share the same coordinator action id (and thus the same queue uniqueness key) but differ only in the entityKey argument. CallableQueueService is expected to accept exactly the first callable that wins the uniqueness claim and drop the rest, but the selection among the three equal-priority callables placed in the queue is determined by nondeterministic internal ordering (hash/DelayQueue ordering) rather than by submission order. When hash ordering is perturbed (NonDex seed 42 / seed 828922), callable2 or callable3 is dequeued and claims uniqueness first, so callable1.executed stays 0 or callable2/3 execute, making the assertions at line 151 fail.

evidence.why: All three commands are constructed with the same actionId but distinct entityKeys and enqueued into CallableQueueService. The test hard-codes the expectation that callable1 is the one that wins the queue-uniqueness claim and executes, while 2 and 3 are silently dropped. This depends entirely on the order in which the queue service processes equal-key/equal-priority entries, which is implementation (hash/DelayQueue) dependent and is exactly what NonDex perturbs.

The failure stack terminates at TestCoordActionInputCheckXCommand.java:151 (junit.framework.Assert.assertTrue), i.e. one of these three order-of-execution assertions fails because a callable other than callable1 won the uniqueness claim under the perturbed non-deterministic queue ordering.
